overview.text: The viola is a bowed string instrument in the violin family, held against the shoulder and played with a bow or by plucking its strings. Larger and lower in sound than the violin, it fills the family’s middle, or alto, register between violin and cello. Its four strings are tuned C–G–D–A, each a perfect fifth apart; the lower strings give it a darker, richer tone. In orchestras and chamber groups, violas support the harmony and connect higher and lower parts, but they can also play melodies and solo passages. Viola music is usually written in alto clef. Historically, “viola” named different instruments, so viola da braccio and viola da gamba are not interchangeable terms.

key_facts.text: The viola’s standard tuning, from lowest to highest, is C–G–D–A.
Viola parts are typically written in alto clef; treble clef may be used for higher passages.
Its middle-register role makes the viola a regular part of both orchestras and chamber ensembles.
The viola’s tone is generally darker and less brilliant than the violin’s, while still allowing agile playing and solo passages.
In historical usage, viola da braccio and viola da gamba referred to distinct instrument traditions; the modern viola belongs to the violin-family line associated with viola da braccio.

overview.text: The harpsichord is a keyboard instrument whose keys lift vertical jacks; a plectrum on each jack plucks a string, producing a bright, crisp sound. In its grand form, its strings run front to back, unlike the horizontally strung virginal or spinet. Pressing a key harder does not make a harpsichord note louder, so it differs from the piano, which uses hammers to strike strings and allows changes in loudness through touch. Harpsichords were played in Renaissance households and became important in Baroque music, both as solo instruments and in basso continuo, where they supplied chords beneath a melody.

key_facts.text: When a key is pressed, its jack rises and a plectrum plucks the string; as the jack falls, the plectrum pivots aside and a damper silences the string.
The harpsichord’s sound is often described as light, bright, and crisp.
Players cannot vary a note’s loudness just by pressing its key harder; the piano instead strikes strings with hammers.
Harpsichords and spinets were among the keyboard instruments found in Renaissance households.
In Baroque music, the harpsichord could serve as a solo instrument or provide basso continuo: chords accompanying a melody and reinforced by a bass instrument.

overview.text: Surrealism is an international literary and arts movement that took shape in 1920s Paris, with writer André Breton as a leading organizer; Breton’s 1924 manifesto helped define its aims. Influenced by Sigmund Freud’s ideas about dreams and the unconscious, Surrealists sought to loosen the control of reason and social convention so hidden thoughts and imaginative associations could surface. They worked in poetry, painting, drawing, photography, film, and design, using methods such as automatic writing or drawing, chance, collage, and startling combinations of familiar things. There was no single Surrealist look: some artists painted precise, dreamlike scenes, while others made spontaneous or abstract forms. René Magritte and Salvador Dalí became prominent visual members.

key_facts.text: Breton’s Manifesto of Surrealism appeared in Paris in 1924, helping establish the movement as an international literary, artistic, and political force.
Surrealist automatism meant creating writing or art with reduced conscious control; artists also used free association and chance.
Surrealism drew on Freud’s ideas about dreams and the unconscious, but its artists used them as creative inspiration—not as a single required subject or style.
Surrealists made work in many forms, including literature, painting, photography, film, design, and objects assembled from existing things.
René Magritte and Salvador Dalí were prominent visual Surrealists; their work illustrates the movement’s range, from carefully rendered, uncanny scenes to hallucinatory imagery.

overview.text: The human voice is the body’s sound-making instrument: air from the lungs passes through the larynx, where paired vocal folds vibrate to create sound. People use that sound for speech, singing, humming, cries, and other vocal expression. Voice is not identical to speech: it is the sound source, while coordinated movements of the tongue and lips shape it into recognizable speech sounds. The throat, mouth, and nose also modify the sound through resonance. The vocal folds and resonating spaces help determine pitch, volume, and tone, contributing to why voices differ. Because it can communicate words and carry melody, the voice is central to communication and music.

key_facts.text: The vocal folds are a pair of tissue bands in the larynx; they are open during quiet breathing and vibrate as air from the lungs passes them during voice production.
Voice is the sound source; speech forms recognizable sounds by coordinating movements of the tongue, lips, and other parts of the vocal tract.
The throat, mouth, and nose act as resonating spaces that modify vocal sound; their size and shape help influence voice quality.
Pitch, volume, and tone are among the qualities that help make voices sound different.
People use the voice for activities including speaking and singing, as well as vocal sounds such as humming and crying.

overview.text: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (1746–1828) was a Spanish painter and printmaker whose long career ranged from royal portraits and lively scenes to stark, unsettling images. He became a court painter, but is especially remembered for works confronting superstition and the human cost of war. His 1799 etching series Los Caprichos used satire and fantasy; The Disasters of War depicted atrocities during Spain’s struggle against French occupation; and The Third of May 1808 shows captured Spaniards facing a French firing squad. Later, at his country house, Quinta del Sordo, he painted the private murals now known as the Black Paintings.

key_facts.text: Goya became completely deaf after an illness in the early 1790s.
He completed and published Los Caprichos in 1799; the series contains 80 allegorical etchings.
The Disasters of War prints were made between 1810 and 1820 and were not published until after Goya’s death.
The Black Paintings were private works made at Quinta del Sordo between 1820 and 1823.

overview.text: Rembrandt van Rijn’s *The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp* is a 1632 group portrait commissioned to show Amsterdam surgeons with Dr Tulp teaching anatomy. Tulp demonstrates the muscles of a dissected forearm while the other surgeons look in different directions, making the gathering feel active rather than like a stiff row of sitters. Strong light-and-dark contrasts help focus attention on the figures. The body is identified as Adriaen Adriaensz, known as Aris Kindt, who was hanged before the dissection. Although the scene depicts an anatomy lesson, medical historians note it should not be treated as an exact record of the dissection: the painting also arranges the surgeons into a commemorative group portrait.

The Amsterdam surgeons’ guild commissioned Rembrandt to portray its members with Dr Nicolaes Tulp.
Tulp demonstrates the forearm’s muscles; the corpse is identified as Aris Kindt, who was hanged on January 31, 1632.
The surgeons’ varied gazes, dynamic arrangement, and strong light-and-dark contrasts distinguish the composition.
The painting presents a group portrait in the form of an anatomy lesson, not necessarily an exact depiction of the dissection itself.

overview.text: Dale Chihuly (born 1941 in Tacoma, Washington) is an American artist who made glass the focus of large-scale sculpture and installation. After studying interior design and glass, he co-founded Pilchuck Glass School in 1971, helping build a center for glass artists. Chihuly develops work with teams of glassblowers, rather than making every piece himself. His well-known series include Baskets, Seaforms, Persians, and Chandeliers. He also places glass in architectural and garden settings, extending sculpture onto walls and ceilings and into outdoor spaces. Projects such as Chihuly Over Venice and his Garden Cycle show how he uses settings as part of the experience of his glass art.

key_facts.text: Chihuly studied interior design at the University of Washington and earned his degree in 1965.
He received a Fulbright Fellowship in 1968 and worked at Venice’s Venini glass factory, where he observed a team approach to glassblowing.
Chihuly co-founded Pilchuck Glass School in Washington State in 1971.
After an automobile accident in 1976 left him without sight in his left eye, Chihuly shifted his way of making art; he has worked with a team of glassblowers.
His series include Cylinders, Baskets, Seaforms, Macchia, Venetians, Persians, Niijima Floats, Chandeliers, and Fiori.

overview.text: Hector Berlioz (1803–1869) was a French Romantic composer and conductor who left medical studies to pursue music. His 1830 Symphonie fantastique tells a dramatic story through five movements: a recurring melody, the idée fixe, represents the beloved of an imagined young artist, while changing orchestral colors help shape the narrative. Berlioz’s fascination with Shakespearean actress Harriet Smithson inspired the work in part, but its plot is a musical program, not a literal account of events. He also composed The Damnation of Faust and wrote a widely influential treatise on instruments and orchestration, treating tone color as an important part of musical expression.

key_facts.text: Berlioz was born in La Côte-Saint-André, France, in 1803; after beginning medical studies in Paris, he chose a career in music.
Symphonie fantastique was composed in 1830 and premiered in Paris on December 5 that year; it has five movements.
In the symphony, the idée fixe—a recurring theme associated with the beloved—returns in different forms across all five movements.
His orchestration treatise describes instruments’ ranges, mechanics, timbres, and expressive possibilities; its first edition appeared in late 1843, though the work is dated 1844.
The Damnation of Faust premiered in Paris in 1846, where its first performance was unsuccessful.

overview.text: The Creation of Adam is a scene in Michelangelo’s frescoed ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City, painted between 1508 and 1512. It presents the biblical account in Genesis of God creating the first human: Adam reclines on the left while God, borne by angels and wrapped in a mantle, reaches toward him. Their meeting fingers form the scene’s focal point, a vivid image of life passing from Creator to human. The panel belongs to a larger sequence of Genesis stories, placed between scenes of creation and the later story of Eve and humanity’s fall. Its striking, simple gesture has made it one of the best-known images of Renaissance art.

key_facts.text: The Vatican Museums identify the scene with Genesis 1:26–27 and describe the life-giving encounter between the Creator and Adam.
The Vatican Museums describe Adam as a resting athlete and God as leaning toward him, supported by angels and wrapped in a mantle.

overview.text: Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669) was a Dutch painter and printmaker whose portraits, history paintings, and prints helped define seventeenth-century Dutch art. Born in Leiden, he trained there and in Amsterdam before moving to Amsterdam around 1632, where he built a successful workshop. Viewers often recognize his work by its dramatic contrasts of light and dark, expressive faces and gestures, and willingness to vary composition and brushwork. His 1642 group portrait, The Night Watch, turns a civic militia portrait into an energetic scene, with figures caught in different actions rather than arranged as a still lineup. He also made technically inventive etchings and drypoints, revising plates to create different effects.

key_facts.text: Rembrandt was born in Leiden in 1606 and died in Amsterdam in 1669.
He trained with Jacob van Swanenburgh in Leiden and Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam; by 1628 he was teaching pupils.

overview.text: Gioachino Rossini (1792–1868) was an Italian composer whose prolific career made him a leading figure in early nineteenth-century opera. Born in Pesaro to musical parents, he studied in Bologna and began his theatrical career in Venice. He wrote both comic operas, including The Barber of Seville and La Cenerentola, and serious works such as Tancredi and William Tell. After working in Italy, Rossini settled in Paris, where William Tell premiered in 1829 as his last opera. He later composed sacred and shorter works, but his best-known achievements remain his operas, notable for spanning comic, serious, and in-between forms.

key_facts.text: Rossini was born in Pesaro on February 29, 1792; his father played horn and trumpet, and his mother was a singer.
He studied music in Bologna and made his theatrical debut in Venice in 1810 with the comic opera La cambiale di matrimonio.
The Barber of Seville premiered in 1816 and La Cenerentola in 1817; both are among his celebrated comic operas.
Rossini also wrote serious opera, including Tancredi; his final opera, William Tell, premiered in Paris in 1829.

overview.text: Burj Khalifa is a mixed-use skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, that opened on January 4, 2010. At 828 meters (2,716.5 feet) to its architectural top, it became the world’s tallest building, a title formally confirmed by the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat in March 2010. Designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, its three wings surround a central core in a Y-shaped plan that helps reduce wind forces; setbacks spiral upward toward a steel spire. Homes, offices, a hotel, and observation decks share the tower, making it a landmark of modern engineering and a defining feature of Dubai’s skyline.

overview.text: Meat is animal flesh eaten as food; in many everyday descriptions, “meat” chiefly means mammals such as cattle, pigs, and sheep, with poultry and seafood often grouped separately. It is a protein-rich food, but the animals people eat and the ways they prepare or avoid meat vary across regions, traditions, religions, and personal values. Plant-based meat alternatives contain plant or fungal ingredients processed to resemble animal meat in qualities such as flavor, texture, or appearance. Cultivated meat is different: it is made by growing animal cells in controlled conditions, then harvesting the resulting material. The key distinction is the source—plant or fungal ingredients versus cultured animal cells—not simply how meat-like a product looks or tastes.

key_facts.text: In common usage, meat often refers to edible mammal flesh; poultry and seafood are also important animal foods and are often discussed separately.
Meat is a protein-rich food that also contains other nutrients.
Food traditions, regional ingredients, religion, and personal values can shape whether and how people eat meat.
Plant-based meat alternatives can use soy, other legumes, or fungi, with processing intended to imitate qualities such as meat’s texture, flavor, or appearance.

overview.text: Sodium chloride (NaCl), usually called common or table salt, is a compound made of sodium and chlorine. Its naturally occurring mineral form is halite, an evaporite: it crystallizes as salty water loses water through evaporation. Halite may occur in underground beds of rock salt, and its broken crystals often have a cube-like shape. People value salt for seasoning and have long used it to help dry and preserve foods. Salt also shaped economies: in Western Europe, common salt was an object of international competition and was important for preserving provisions on long-distance voyages. Thus, an everyday kitchen ingredient links mineral formation, food technology, and trade.

overview.text: Haiti is a Caribbean country occupying the western part of Hispaniola, the second-largest island in the Greater Antilles; the Dominican Republic occupies the rest. Its capital is Port-au-Prince. Haiti’s two long peninsulas give its outline a distinctive horseshoe shape, and its territory includes offshore islands such as Gonâve. Much of the land is mountainous, with river valleys and small coastal plains; Haiti is described as the most mountainous nation in the Caribbean. Five mountain ranges shape its landscape, which is commonly divided into northern, central, and southern regions. These contrasts between ridges, valleys, and coastal lowlands define Haiti’s physical geography.

overview.text: The Alps are a major mountain system in south-central Europe, curving in a broad arc from the Ligurian Sea and southeastern France eastward toward Slovenia and the Adriatic. The Alpine Convention identifies an Alpine region spanning eight countries: Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Slovenia, and Switzerland. The range is distinguished by high, rugged folded mountains, including Mont Blanc, and by its importance as a source area for major rivers such as the Rhine, Rhône, and Po. The Alps formed through tectonic compression and uplift associated with the collision of the Adriatic microplate and Eurasian Plate; mountain passes have long connected northern and Mediterranean Europe.

overview.text: Connecticut is a small, southernmost state of New England, bordered by New York, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and Long Island Sound. The Connecticut River flows south through the state, roughly dividing it; flatter coastal and central areas contrast with forested hills, especially in the northwest. Its history links colonial New England to the founding United States: chartered as a colony in 1662, Connecticut became the fifth state to ratify the U.S. Constitution, on January 9, 1788. Hartford is now its capital and has been the sole capital city since 1875. The state adopted “The Constitution State” as its official designation in 1959.

overview.text: Colombia, officially the Republic of Colombia, occupies the northwestern corner of South America; its capital, Bogotá, stands high in the Andes. The country is especially varied in landforms: geographers distinguish six natural regions—Andean, Caribbean, Pacific, Orinoquía, Amazonian, and Insular. In the west, the Andes divide into three cordilleras, with the Cauca and Magdalena river valleys between them. Northern lowlands reach the Caribbean, while the Pacific region lies to the west; broad plains and savannas extend east toward Amazonian rainforest. These sharp contrasts in elevation and landscape help make Colombia’s geography distinctive, from mountain valleys and highlands to tropical coasts and forests.

overview.text: Central Park is a major public park in Manhattan, New York City, created to provide recreation and a countryside-like retreat for residents of a rapidly growing city. Its winning Greensward Plan, designed by landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, blended open lawns, woodlands, lakes, and paths with bridges and roads arranged to let traffic pass through without spoiling the park experience. The park’s 843 acres include distinct landscapes such as the Ramble, a deliberately designed woodland with winding trails, a stream, and rocky outcrops. Its influential design helped shape urban parks nationwide. The site also has a human history: creating the park displaced residents, including people from Seneca Village, a predominantly African American community.

Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux’s Greensward Plan won a design competition; it combined naturalistic scenery with formal features and bridges.

overview.text: Nome is a city at the southern edge of Alaska’s Seward Peninsula; its local Iñupiaq name is Sitnasuaq. Its modern growth began with a gold discovery near Anvil Creek in 1898, followed by gold found in beach sands the next year, helping turn it into a boomtown. Archaeological evidence also documents human use of the area long before gold seekers arrived. Nome is a regional hub and the finish city of the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race: the first race to Nome took place in 1973. The historic trail served as a route for mail and supplies, and part of it was used in the 1925 sled-dog serum relay to Nome.

overview.text: The Tigris is one of the two great rivers associated with Mesopotamia, alongside the Euphrates. It rises in eastern Turkey’s Taurus Mountains, receives much of its water from snowmelt, and flows south through Turkey into Iraq. In Iraq, it passes Baghdad, a major city on its banks. Farther south, the Tigris joins the Euphrates in the Shatt al-Arab waterway, which empties into the Persian Gulf. The river has long mattered because its water supports irrigation, farming, travel, and settlement in a region where water is especially valuable.

overview.text: The Red Sea is a long, narrow tropical sea between northeastern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. At its northern end, the Sinai Peninsula separates it into the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba; the Gulf of Suez connects to the Mediterranean through Egypt’s Suez Canal. In the south, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait leads to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. This position makes the Red Sea part of a major shipping route between Europe and Asia. It is also a rift basin shaped by the movement of the African and Arabian tectonic plates, and its warm waters support extensive coral reefs and distinctive marine life.

overview.text: George Gordon Byron (1788–1824), known as Lord Byron, was an English poet and leading figure of the Romantic movement. His aristocratic title and public image made him a celebrated, controversial figure, but his reputation rests especially on poems that combine vivid narrative, personal feeling, political interest, and satire. Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, partly shaped by his travels, brought him wide fame in 1812. In contrast, Don Juan turns the legendary lover’s story into a comic, sharply critical narrative poem, using the playful eight-line ottava rima stanza; Byron left it unfinished. His writings helped shape the influential “Byronic hero,” while his support for Greek independence linked his literary fame to political action; he died in Greece.

The first two cantos of Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage appeared in 1812 and quickly made him famous.

overview.text: In “To a Mouse,” Robert Burns addresses a field mouse whose nest has been overturned by a plough, expressing regret that human activity has disrupted nature. The poem follows the mouse’s ruined shelter as winter approaches, then widens into a reflection on how plans can fail for both animals and people. Its closing contrast suggests that the mouse lives in the present, while the speaker worries about the past and future. Burns’s Scots wording—such as “wee” and “gang aft agley”—gives the poem a distinctive voice. First published in 1786, it is known for its sympathy toward the mouse and inspired the title of John Steinbeck’s *Of Mice and Men*.

overview.text: “Song of Myself” is Walt Whitman’s long poem, first published in 1855 as one of twelve untitled poems in Leaves of Grass; it later became known by its familiar title. Its 52 sections move through scenes of nature, bodily experience, work, death, and encounters with other people. The speaker begins by celebrating himself but repeatedly connects his own life with the reader’s and with a broad human community, making the self both individual and shared. Whitman’s experimental free verse and sweeping, energetic voice helped establish a distinctly American poetic style. The poem’s final section ends with its defiant image of a “barbaric yawp,” a phrase that captures its bold, public voice.

Encounters with a paint factory and the Brotherhood, an organization claiming to help oppressed people, mix social critique with surreal and sometimes comic episodes. His underground refuge frames an ongoing search for identity and self-determination. Recognized as an important work of American literature, the novel explores African American life amid unequal treatment; Ellison became the first Black author to win the National Book Award, in 1953.

overview.text: Alexandre Dumas père (1802–1870)—“père” distinguishes him from his son, Alexandre Dumas fils—was a French novelist and playwright born in Villers-Cotterêts. His best-known novels include The Three Musketeers (1844) and The Count of Monte Cristo (1845–46). In The Three Musketeers, Dumas reshaped earlier memoir-like material into a lively fictional world featuring d’Artagnan, Athos, Porthos, and Aramis; the Académie française notes that collaborator Auguste Maquet drafted an early version, which Dumas revised and reworked. Historical settings, suspense, humor, and memorable companions helped make these stories lasting landmarks of popular literature.

overview.text: The Epic of Gilgamesh is an ancient Mesopotamian epic centered on Gilgamesh, a legendary king of Uruk. overview.text: “The Lottery” is Shirley Jackson’s short story, first published in The New Yorker in 1948. It begins in an ordinary-looking village on a bright summer morning, where neighbors gather for an annual drawing organized around a shabby black box and folded slips of paper. Jackson gradually reveals that the “winner” is selected for death: the black-spotted slip identifies Tessie Hutchinson, whom the villagers stone. The calm, matter-of-fact narration and the children’s early collection of stones make the turn especially chilling. The story remains significant for its unsettling portrait of communal violence and unexamined tradition. overview.text: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa’s “Rashōmon,” first published in 1915, is a Japanese short story set in a decaying Kyoto during the late twelfth century. When she defends her act as necessary to avoid starvation, the servant uses her reasoning to justify stripping her of her kimono. Its bleak setting and compact confrontation make survival and ethical compromise its defining concerns.

overview.text: An autobiography is nonfiction life-writing in which a person retrospectively narrates their own life—or a substantial part of it—rather than someone else’s life, as in biography. It often uses first-person prose, but there is no single required structure: autobiographical works can vary in form and scope. The author does more than list events, selecting and arranging memories to interpret personal identity and development within a social and historical setting. This makes autobiography a literary way to view both an individual’s experience and the world around them, though memory and selection mean it is not a complete, neutral record. “Memoir” is sometimes used interchangeably, but more often focuses on a particular period or theme.

overview.text: “The Minister’s Black Veil: A Parable” is a short story by American writer Nathaniel Hawthorne, included in his 1837 collection Twice-Told Tales. Set in the New England village of Milford, it follows Reverend Mr. Hooper after he appears at church wearing a black crape veil that hides most of his face. The congregation’s fear and his fiancée Elizabeth’s questions make the veil a sign of separation and secrecy; Hooper connects it to hidden sin shared by humanity. Yet Hawthorne never reveals a private offense as the veil’s definite cause. That uncertainty is central: the veil works as a disturbing symbol of what people conceal from one another and themselves, rather than a simple clue to a single secret.

overview.text: The Basel problem asks for the exact sum of the infinite series 1/1² + 1/2² + 1/3² + …, whose terms are reciprocals of the positive integers’ squares. Its unexpected answer is π²/6: a question about whole-number squares turns out to involve π, the circle constant. Mathematicians including members of the Bernoulli family had worked on the sum; the name reflects Basel and that family’s association with the city. Leonhard Euler solved the problem in 1735, a celebrated early achievement that helped establish his reputation. The result remains a subject of mathematical study, with researchers continuing to publish different proofs.

overview.text: In mathematics, a limit describes the value that a function’s outputs approach as its input nears a chosen point, or that a sequence’s terms approach as its index grows. The key is nearby behavior, not necessarily the value at the point: a function may be undefined there, or its defined value may differ from its limit. For a two-sided function limit, outputs from both sides must approach the same finite value; otherwise, no such finite limit exists. Limits are foundational to calculus: continuity at a point requires the limit to equal the function’s value there, and the derivative is defined using a limit of slopes of nearby secant lines.

key_facts.text: The notation lim indicates a limit; for a function, x→a means examining outputs as inputs approach a, not necessarily at a.
A function’s limit can differ from its value at the point, and the function need not be defined at that point for the limit to exist.
A sequence is a function on the positive integers; its limit describes how its terms behave as the index n grows.
Continuity at a point requires that the function be defined there, that its limit exist, and that the limit equal the function’s value.
A derivative uses a limit: secant-line slopes approach the tangent-line slope as the second point moves toward the first.

overview.text: Geometric congruence describes figures that match exactly in shape and size: one can be placed onto the other with no stretching or resizing. A translation (slide), rotation (turn), or reflection (flip) may change a figure’s position or orientation without changing its measurements, so corresponding side lengths and angle measures remain equal. A mirror image can therefore still be congruent. This differs from similarity, which allows figures to have the same shape but different sizes. Congruence helps identify exact matches in patterns and is useful in proving triangles match: rules such as SSS and SAS let certain corresponding measurements establish triangle congruence without measuring every part.

overview.text: Expected value, also called expectation or the mean, is a number that summarizes a random variable by weighting its possible values according to their probabilities. For a discrete variable, multiply each possible value by its probability and add; for a continuous variable with density f(x), the corresponding calculation is the integral of x f(x) over its range. It is commonly written E[X] or E(X), and is the first moment. Expected value can describe an average over many repetitions, but it need not be an outcome of any single trial: a fair six-sided die has expected value 3.5, although no roll shows 3.5.

overview.text: The natural logarithm, written ln x, is the logarithm to base e: it answers the question “to what power must e be raised to produce x?” For positive x, it can also be defined by the integral ln x = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt, making its value the signed area under y = 1/t between 1 and x. This definition explains its key calculus role: its derivative is 1/x, so an antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x| + C on any interval that does not cross zero. The number e is characterized by ln e = 1, and ln is the inverse of the exponential function eˣ.

overview.text: Walter Elias Disney (1901–1966) was an American animator, filmmaker, and producer who started an animation business with his brother Roy after moving to Hollywood in 1923. He became widely associated with Mickey Mouse: Walt conceived the character, while artist Ub Iwerks further developed it and animated the early cartoons. Mickey’s public debut in Steamboat Willie (1928), one of the first cartoons to use synchronized sound successfully, helped establish the studio. Disney’s influence also came from treating animation as feature-length storytelling. Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) was his studio’s first feature—not the first animated feature ever—and combined expressive character animation, music, color, and a carefully developed story. Disney later helped create Disneyland, which opened in 1955.

key_facts.text: In 1923, Walt and Roy Disney began a production operation in Hollywood, making Alice Comedies shorts.
Walt conceived Mickey Mouse, and Ub Iwerks further developed the character; Steamboat Willie gave Mickey his first public appearance on November 18, 1928.

Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs was the Disney studio’s first feature-length film, but it was not the first animated feature. Its blend of animation techniques, color, music, and story helped make it a landmark.
Disney’s 1930s Silly Symphonies shorts served as a testing ground for animation advances, including color and techniques that created an illusion of depth.
Disneyland, the theme park Disney pursued with his team, opened on July 17, 1955.

overview.text: Satyrs are male nature spirits in Greek mythology, imagined as humanlike beings with animal features. Their appearance varies across art: some Greek depictions give them horse-like ears and tails, while other portrayals show goatlike legs, ears, or horns. They were linked with woodland settings and often accompanied Dionysus (also called Bacchus), the god of wine and theater. Artists commonly show them with music, wine, dancing, and celebration. Satyrs also became figures in Greek theater: satyr plays used a chorus of satyrs and brought comic, earthy contrast to tragic myths. Vase paintings and sculpture show how artists reimagined these spirits over time.

key_facts.text: Satyr imagery was not uniform: some Greek representations show horse-like ears and tails, while other art gives satyrs goatlike features.
Satyrs often accompanied Dionysus, the wine god; art shows them with pipes, wine vessels, or dancing in celebration.
Satyr plays featured a satyr chorus and were performed after a trio of tragedies, adding comedy to mythic subjects.
A mid-fifth-century BCE Attic red-figure cup fragment at the Met depicts satyrs with a maenad and drinking or Dionysian attributes.
A Greek terracotta statuette at the Met, dated to the late fourth–early third century BCE, shows a satyr wearing a wreath and holding a cornucopia.

overview.text: Kashrut, also spelled kashruth, is the Jewish system of dietary laws and practices; “kosher” means fit or permitted under that system. Its scriptural foundations include the Torah’s classifications of animals, while rabbinic interpretation developed further rules for preparing, slaughtering, and serving food—so kosher status concerns more than ingredients alone. Distinctive rules include permitting land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, allowing fish with fins and scales, and separating meat and dairy, often with separate utensils. Foods that are neither meat nor dairy are called pareve. Kashrut connects everyday eating with Jewish religious tradition, though observance and interpretation differ among Jewish communities.

key_facts.text: “Kosher” means “fit” or “proper”; it describes food permitted under kashrut.
The Torah provides kashrut’s scriptural foundations; rabbinic interpretation added rules about food preparation, slaughter, and separating meat and dairy.
Among the permitted foods, land animals must chew the cud and have split hooves; kosher fish have fins and scales.
Meat and dairy are kept separate, often using separate dishes and utensils; foods that are neither are commonly called pareve.

For meat to be kosher, the FAQ describes ritual slaughter called shechitah and removal of blood; it also notes that observance and discussion of kashrut have developed differently across Jewish movements.

overview.text: Joseph Campbell’s The Hero with a Thousand Faces is a comparative mythology book first published by Pantheon Books in 1949. Drawing on myths, folklore, religion, and modern psychology, Campbell proposed a “monomyth”: a recurring hero-story pattern that he believed appeared across cultures. Its central movement is departure from familiar life, initiation through trials and transformation, and return; the pattern can include crossing into a strange or supernatural realm, gaining a boon, and bringing something back. The book also examines myths of creation and cosmic dissolution. Its lasting significance is that it gave readers and storytellers an influential lens for comparing narratives, including modern films. Campbell’s model is an interpretation, not a rule that every culture’s stories must follow.

key_facts.text: The first edition was published in 1949 by Pantheon Books as part of the Bollingen Series.
Campbell called his pattern the “monomyth,” a term he borrowed from writer James Joyce.
Campbell described its basic arc as departure, initiation, and return, while allowing for variations in the stages.
The book also presents the Cosmogonic Cycle, a pattern about the creation and dissolution of worlds.
Campbell’s claim of a recurring pattern across cultures is a comparative theory, not a fixed formula every story must follow; scholars have debated claims about literary universals.

overview.text: Excalibur is the legendary sword associated with King Arthur, a ruler whose stories became a major part of medieval literature. Its significance varies by version, but it is often tied to rightful kingship and supernatural aid. In Thomas Malory’s *Le Morte d’Arthur*, Arthur first draws a sword from a stone; after that sword breaks, the Lady of the Lake gives him Excalibur. Thus, in Malory, the two swords are distinct, though other tellings connect or combine the motifs. Malory also gives Excalibur a magical scabbard that prevents its wearer from bleeding. The sword’s shifting origins show how Arthurian storytellers reshaped the legend over time.

key_facts.text: In Malory’s story, Arthur pulls a sword from a stone to demonstrate his right to rule, then later receives Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake.
Other medieval tellings connect the sword-in-the-stone episode with Excalibur; a 13th-century French manuscript depicts Arthur drawing Excalibur from an anvil or stone.
Malory says Excalibur’s scabbard keeps its wearer from losing blood, even when badly wounded.
Arthurian stories developed across medieval texts: the British Library describes later writers adding episodes about Merlin, the Round Table, and Arthur’s knights.
In Malory’s account, Arthur takes Excalibur and its scabbard from a barge beside a lake after Merlin directs him to the Lady of the Lake.

overview.text: The Calydonian Boar Hunt is a Greek myth about a dangerous beast sent to ravage the countryside around Calydon. In the version summarized by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Artemis sends the boar after King Oeneus fails to include her in his offerings; Oeneus’s son Meleager gathers famous Greek hunters to stop it. The hunt is especially remembered for Atalanta, a skilled huntress who wounds the boar first, and Meleager, who delivers the fatal blow. Meleager then awards her the animal’s pelt, a decision that leads to a quarrel over the prize. The story’s dramatic hunt and trophy-giving scene inspired later artworks.

key_facts.text: The myth places the hunt in the countryside of Calydon; Artemis sends the boar after King Oeneus omits her from his offerings.
Meleager assembles a band of celebrated Greek heroes to hunt the beast.
Atalanta is the huntress who wounds the boar first; Meleager kills it.
Meleager gives Atalanta the boar’s pelt, provoking a dispute with his uncles over the trophy.
Later artists depicted both the pursuit and the aftermath, including Meleager presenting the boar’s head to Atalanta.

overview.text: Xibalba (also spelled Xibalbá and sometimes called “Place of Fear”) is the underworld in Maya myth, especially the K’iche’ Maya tradition recorded in the Popol Vuh. The Getty describes it as a realm below earth associated with death and powerful rulers. In this story, underworld lords challenge the Hero Twins, who ultimately defeat them through cunning rather than strength. Xibalba therefore forms the setting for a major encounter between the twins and death-associated powers. The myth’s influence is also explored through Maya ceramics: museum specialists connect some Classic-period vessels with underworld figures and possible Popol Vuh episodes, though identifying exact scenes can remain uncertain.

overview.text: The Lord’s Prayer, also called the Our Father or Pater Noster, is a central Christian prayer that Christian scripture presents as taught by Jesus. Matthew places it within the Sermon on the Mount, while Luke gives a shorter version after a disciple asks Jesus how to pray. The prayer addresses God as “Our Father” and moves through requests concerning God’s name and kingdom, daily needs, forgiveness, and protection from evil. Its use of “our” makes it a shared, communal prayer. The two Gospel versions differ in wording and length, and Christian traditions vary in how they conclude it.

key_facts.text: The prayer appears in Matthew 6:9–13 and Luke 11:2–4; the Vatican Catechism describes Matthew’s form as seven petitions and Luke’s as five.
In Matthew, it follows Jesus’ teaching against showy prayer and begins with an instruction to pray in this manner.
Its petitions include God’s name and kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil or testing; wording differs among versions.

The early Christian Didache also records a version and instructs its readers to pray it three times daily; this is evidence of what that text prescribed, not proof of how widely the practice was followed.
The Didache’s version shares phrases and themes with Jewish prayers, while its wording differs from the versions in Matthew and Luke.

overview.text: Parvati is a major Hindu goddess, known especially as Shiva’s consort and as the mother of Ganesha and Skanda (also called Kartikeya). Hindu stories and images present her as both a partner in Shiva’s divine life and a nurturing figure at the heart of their family; some accounts describe her as Sati reborn. She also appears beside Shiva in Ardhanari, a shared form that represents the divine as both female and male. South Indian Somaskanda sculptures make these family relationships visible, placing Parvati and Shiva on either side of their son Skanda. Such images are devotional art as well as depictions of mythological figures.

key_facts.text: A Museum of Fine Arts, Houston account describes Parvati as Sati, Shiva’s first consort, reborn; this is a mythological tradition, not a historical claim.

In Ardhanari, Parvati and Shiva share one form, representing the divine as both female and male.
A South Indian Somaskanda sculpture shows Parvati and Shiva with Skanda between them; The Met describes this as a popular religious image in South India.

overview.text: In Sikhism, Guru denotes an authoritative spiritual guide who conveys divine wisdom; the title has a specific meaning in the tradition beyond its general use for a teacher. Sikh history recognizes ten human Gurus, beginning with Guru Nanak, who founded the faith in Punjab in the late fifteenth century. The human succession ended with Guru Gobind Singh in 1708. Sikhs recognize the Guru Granth Sahib—their sacred scripture—as the eternal Guru and continuing spiritual authority. This transition distinguishes Sikh Guruship: spiritual guidance continues through the scripture rather than a successor in human form. The Gurus’ teachings are central to Sikhism and are enshrined in the Guru Granth Sahib.

key_facts.text: The ten human Gurus begin with Guru Nanak and end with Guru Gobind Singh.
Guru Nanak founded Sikhism in Punjab in the late fifteenth century; nine successors followed him.
Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa in 1699.
In 1708, Guru Gobind Singh passed Guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib, ending the line of personal Gurus.
Sikhs regard the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru; Sikh teachings are enshrined in it.

overview.text: Ahimsa (also spelled ahinsa) means nonviolence or non-harming, and while recognized in several South Asian traditions, it is especially central in Jainism. Jain teaching links this ethic to the belief that living beings, including plants and animals, have souls; practitioners therefore seek to reduce harm rather than assume it can always be eliminated. Ahimsa is more than avoiding physical injury: Jain vows encompass thought, speech, and action, and prohibit causing or approving harm as well as doing it oneself. Its everyday expressions include vegetarian choices and careful movement to avoid injuring small creatures. It is the first of five vows that shape both monastic commitments and lay ethics.

key_facts.text: Ahimsa means nonviolence and is also important in Hindu and Buddhist traditions; Jain teaching makes it a foundation of religious life.
Jain teaching regards humans, animals, and plants as ensouled beings, extending the ethic of non-harm across forms of life.
Ahimsa is the first of five Jain vows, alongside truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity, and non-possession.
The vow concerns harm in thought, speech, and action, including causing harm or consenting to it.
Vegetarian choices and precautions against injuring insects are examples of ahimsa in daily life; Jain renouncers may take especially careful steps.
The Metropolitan Museum describes the motionless standing meditation posture kayotsarga as an expression of ahimsa: stillness is intended to prevent harm even to tiny creatures.

overview.text: Gungnir is Odin’s named spear in Norse mythology. In Snorri Sturluson’s Prose Edda, dwarves called Ívaldi’s Sons make the spear, which becomes Odin’s possession. The Hávamál describes Odin hanging on a tree for nine nights, wounded by a spear, and gaining runes; that passage does not name either the spear or the tree. The Swedish History Museum identifies them as Gungnir and Yggdrasil in its account of Odin’s ordeal. Gungnir’s importance therefore lies not only in its connection to a god of war, but also in the mythic story of Odin’s self-sacrifice in pursuit of wisdom.

overview.text: Earth’s mantle is the mostly solid, silicate-rich layer between the thin crust and the core. About 2,900 kilometers thick, it makes up most of Earth’s interior. It is not a global ocean of molten rock: under the intense heat and pressure underground, solid mantle rock can deform and creep extremely slowly. Heat-driven movement within the mantle transfers energy toward the surface and helps drive plate tectonics, including seafloor spreading. In some hotspot models, heat rising through the mantle contributes to volcanic activity, though magma forms at shallower depths. Scientists continue to investigate the details of mantle circulation and the origins of hotspots.

key_facts.text: The mantle lies between Earth’s crust and core; the Moho marks its upper boundary, and the core–mantle boundary is roughly 2,900 kilometers below the surface.
Mantle rocks are mostly silicates, including minerals such as olivine, garnet, and pyroxene.
The mantle is mostly solid, but its rock can deform and flow very slowly under deep-Earth conditions; the asthenosphere is a relatively weak, ductile region in the upper mantle.
Mantle convection transfers heat and material; it is associated with plate tectonics and processes such as seafloor spreading.

A USGS explanation of the Hawaiian hotspot describes solid mantle rising as heat moves upward, with magma forming at shallower depths; the proposed origin of hotspots is a scientific model, not a settled explanation for every hotspot.

overview.text: Soybean (Glycine max), also called soya, is an annual plant in the legume family, cultivated for its protein- and oil-rich seeds. Its leaves usually have three leaflets, and its roots can form nodules with bacteria that convert nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use. People eat soybeans in many ways: young harvested beans are edamame, while processed beans are used for tofu, tempeh, soy drinks and other foods. Soybean oil is used in cooking and processed foods, and the protein-rich meal left after oil extraction is widely used in animal feed. Evidence suggests soybean was domesticated in China, though the precise history remains under study.

key_facts.text: Soybean is the cultivated species Glycine max in the Fabaceae, or legume, family; it is an annual crop.
Its foliage leaves are usually made up of three leaflets, and fine hairs can occur on the leaves, stems and pods.
Root nodules house bacteria that turn atmospheric nitrogen into a form available to plants; this helps explain why soybean is useful in crop rotations.
Edamame is soybean harvested as a vegetable while the pods are still green; mature soybeans are harvested as dry seeds.
Soybeans are processed into foods including tofu, tempeh, soy sauce and soy drinks; soybean oil and protein-rich meal also have major food and feed uses.

overview.text: Malaria is a potentially life-threatening infection caused by Plasmodium parasites and usually transmitted when an infected female Anopheles mosquito bites a person. The parasite’s unusual life cycle passes between two hosts: after entering a human, it first develops in liver cells and then multiplies in red blood cells; another mosquito can pick it up while feeding. Fever, chills, and headache are common early symptoms, but illness can become severe, especially with P. falciparum. Five Plasmodium species are known to cause human malaria. Unlike colds or flu, malaria is not ordinarily spread directly from person to person, and prompt diagnosis and treatment can prevent severe outcomes.

key_facts.text: Only female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit human malaria, and only some Anopheles species carry the parasites.
In humans, the parasite develops first in liver cells, then multiplies in red blood cells; blood-stage parasites cause the illness’s symptoms.
Early symptoms commonly include fever, chills, and headache, often beginning about 10–15 days after an infectious bite.
P. falciparum is the deadliest malaria parasite species; untreated infection can progress to severe illness and death.
Malaria can be diagnosed with a blood test and treated with prescription medicines; prompt care can help prevent severe illness.

overview.text: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave as it crosses between materials where it travels at different speeds; light is a familiar example. At an angled boundary, a speed change makes the ray turn, while the direction of bending depends on whether it slows or speeds up. For light, the refractive index n = c/v compares its speed in a vacuum with its speed in a material, and Snell’s law (n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂) predicts the angles, measured from the perpendicular (normal) to the boundary. Refraction explains why a pencil partly submerged in water can look bent and enables lenses in eyeglasses and telescopes to redirect light.

key_facts.text: The refractive index of a material is the speed of light in a vacuum divided by its speed in that material: n = c/v.
For light entering a slower medium at an angle, the ray bends toward the perpendicular; entering a faster medium bends it away.
Snell’s law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, relates the indices of refraction to the ray’s angles in each medium; those angles are measured from the perpendicular to the boundary.
Different refractive indices in air and water make a pencil partly submerged in water appear discontinuous or bent.
Refraction is used by lenses in eyeglasses and refracting telescopes to redirect light.

overview.text: Rickets is a disorder of growing bones in which bone tissue fails to mineralize normally, leaving bones soft, weak, and sometimes deformed. It most commonly follows too little vitamin D, which helps the body absorb calcium, but too little calcium or phosphate can also cause it. Some cases are inherited or linked to conditions affecting mineral balance, so rickets is not always simply a dietary deficiency. Children may have bone pain, poor growth, or bowed legs and other skeletal changes. Rickets matters because disrupted mineralization during growth can alter a developing skeleton; treatment aims to correct the underlying nutrient shortage or other cause.

key_facts.text: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium; low calcium or phosphate can also contribute to rickets.
Possible signs include bone pain, impaired growth, bowed legs, and other skeletal changes.
Not all rickets is nutritional: inherited forms and conditions affecting mineral balance can also cause it.
Rickets affects children whose bones are still growing; vitamin D deficiency in teens and adults is associated instead with osteomalacia.
Treatment is directed at correcting the cause, such as replacing deficient vitamin D, calcium, or phosphorus.

overview.text: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a group of inherited red-blood-cell disorders caused by gene variants that produce abnormal hemoglobin. Hemoglobin normally carries oxygen; in SCD, hemoglobin can make red cells rigid and sickle- or crescent-shaped. These cells may break down early and stick in small blood vessels, reducing blood flow and contributing to anemia, pain, and organ complications. SCD includes different inherited forms: HbSS and combinations of HbS with another abnormal hemoglobin can cause disease, with severity that varies. By contrast, sickle cell trait usually means one HbS gene and one HbA gene; it is not SCD. Trait is associated with partial protection against severe malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, but it does not guarantee immunity.

key_facts.text: SCD is inherited; a child receives genes for abnormal hemoglobin from their parents.
SCD includes several forms, such as HbSS and HbSC; their severity can differ.
Sickled red cells can break down early and block small blood vessels, contributing to anemia, pain, and other complications.
Sickle cell trait usually means inheriting one HbS gene and one HbA gene; it is distinct from SCD.
Sickle cell trait is associated with partial protection against severe malaria, but people with the trait can still get malaria.

overview.text: Schrödinger’s cat is a 1935 thought experiment by physicist Erwin Schrödinger, devised to expose a puzzle in applying quantum mechanics to everyday-sized things. In the imagined setup, a cat shares a sealed chamber with a radioactive atom, a Geiger counter, and a poison-release mechanism: a decay triggers the counter and releases poison, while no decay leaves the cat alive. Quantum theory assigns probabilities to the atom’s decay; when its uncertain outcome is linked to the cat, the mathematical description includes both alive and dead possibilities before a result is determined. Schrödinger used this deliberately unsettling case to question how quantum descriptions relate to observable reality. It is an illustration, not a real experiment or a claim that ordinary cats literally occupy both conditions.

key_facts.text: In Schrödinger’s imagined mechanism, a radioactive decay sets off a Geiger counter and hammer that breaks a flask of poison; without a decay, the cat lives.
The thought experiment links an uncertain event at the atomic scale to two possible outcomes for a much larger system: the cat alive or dead.
Schrödinger described the example as a deliberately ‘ridiculous’ case to highlight concerns about extending quantum descriptions to visible, everyday objects.
The example raises questions about measurement: a detector can record the atomic event, while the interpretation of what happens to the combined system is part of the puzzle.
The cat is imaginary; the thought experiment is used to explain quantum ideas, not to suggest that real cats are literally both alive and dead.

overview.text: Osteoporosis is a disease in which bone mineral density or mass falls, or bone structure changes, making bones weaker and more likely to fracture. Bone is living tissue that is continually renewed; when breakdown outpaces replacement, its inner honeycomb-like structure thins and the spaces widen. Often there are no warning symptoms until a break occurs, sometimes after a minor fall or even a cough; hip, spine, and wrist are frequent fracture sites. It can affect people of any sex or background, but risk rises with age and is higher in women after menopause. A low-dose DXA/DEXA scan measures bone minerals and helps identify osteoporosis and estimate fracture risk; osteopenia is low bone density less severe than osteoporosis.

key_facts.text: When bone breakdown exceeds replacement, the inner bone structure thins, its spaces grow, and the outer shell becomes thinner—weakening the bone.
Osteoporosis is often symptomless until a fracture; in weakened bones, a minor fall or ordinary stress such as coughing can sometimes cause one.
Fractures commonly affect the hip, spine, or wrist. Spinal fractures may cause severe back pain, height loss, or a hunched posture.
Risk rises with age; other risk factors include low estrogen after menopause, family history, too little calcium or vitamin D, inactivity, and long-term use of some medicines.
A DXA/DEXA scan uses low-dose X-rays to measure bone minerals. Results can help diagnose osteoporosis and assess future fracture risk.

overview.text: Ohm’s law relates the voltage drop across an electrical component, the current through it, and its resistance: V = IR. It is useful for calculating any one of these quantities when the other two are known, helping describe and analyze simple circuits. The relationship reflects experiments by German physicist Georg Simon Ohm in the 19th century. It is an empirical rule, not a pattern every material or component follows: when a component’s current is proportional to voltage over a range of conditions, it is called ohmic. For an ohmic component, doubling voltage while resistance stays constant doubles current.

key_facts.text: In V = IR, V is voltage, I is current, and R is resistance; the same relationship can be rearranged to find any one of them.
Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω); one ohm equals one volt per ampere (1 Ω = 1 V/A).
Ohm’s law describes an experimentally observed relationship; it does not apply to every material or component in all conditions.
A material or component that follows the proportional voltage-current relationship is called ohmic.
Georg Simon Ohm, a German physicist, experimentally established the relationship in the 19th century.

overview.text: Archaea are a domain of single-celled prokaryotes—organisms whose cells lack a nucleus—and one of three major branches of life, alongside Bacteria and Eukarya. Though they can look like bacteria, they are distinct: their cell membranes have ether-linked, branched lipids, and their cell walls lack bacterial peptidoglycan. Comparisons of ribosomal RNA helped Carl Woese and colleagues identify Archaea as a separate evolutionary lineage, changing how scientists organized the tree of life. Archaea live in ordinary as well as extreme environments. Some, called methanogens, make methane as they obtain energy in oxygen-free conditions, including in some animal digestive systems.

key_facts.text: Archaea are unicellular prokaryotes, meaning their cells lack a nucleus; they are classified separately from Bacteria and Eukarya.
Their membranes contain ether-linked branched lipids, and their cell walls lack peptidoglycan, a key component of bacterial cell walls.
Ribosomal RNA comparisons helped Carl Woese and colleagues distinguish Archaea as a separate evolutionary lineage.
Archaea occur in many habitats; extreme heat, cold, or salinity is characteristic of some, not all, members of the domain.
Methanogens are archaea that produce methane in oxygen-free environments; some live in the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

overview.text: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is an aqueous solution of hydrogen chloride, a gas; it is an inorganic, strong acid. In water, HCl dissociates essentially completely into hydronium and chloride ions, which explains its “strong acid” classification—strength refers to ionization, not simply how concentrated a sample is. In the body, gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid as part of stomach acid, which helps digestion alongside enzymes. Beyond biology, it is an important industrial chemical: uses include cleaning oxide from steel (“pickling”), processing ores, producing other chemicals, and adjusting water pH. Hydrochloric acid is corrosive, so laboratory and industrial use requires appropriate controls.

overview.text: 1P/Halley, commonly called Halley’s Comet, is an icy, dusty object that orbits the Sun on a long, stretched path. As it nears the Sun, warming releases gas and dust that form a hazy cloud and tails. Its average orbit takes about 76 years, though the interval varies. English astronomer Edmond Halley compared observations from 1531, 1607, and 1682 and argued in 1705 that they showed one returning comet; he correctly predicted its 1758 return. The comet appeared in 1066 and is depicted on the Bayeux Tapestry, which tells the story of the Norman conquest of England. In 1986, ESA’s Giotto spacecraft captured the first close-up images of a comet nucleus—Halley’s.

key_facts.text: NASA classifies Halley as a short-period comet: its orbit takes less than 200 years.
Its orbital period averages about 76 years, but NASA reports past intervals ranging from 74.42 to 79.25 years.
Halley’s 1705 prediction was based on similarities among comet observations from 1531, 1607, and 1682; the comet returned in 1758.
Dust and rocky material shed by Halley contributes to the Eta Aquariid and Orionid meteor showers.
During its 1986 encounter, ESA’s Giotto mission obtained the first close-up images of a comet nucleus and revealed Halley’s shape and active jets.

overview.text: Triton is Neptune’s largest moon, discovered by British astronomer William Lassell in 1846. Its defining oddity is a retrograde orbit: it circles Neptune opposite the planet’s rotation, unlike other large moons in the solar system. This unusual path, together with similarities to Pluto, supports the idea that Triton formed in the Kuiper Belt and was later captured by Neptune; capture is an inference, not something observed directly. Voyager 2’s 1989 flyby revealed an icy, nitrogen-rich world with active geysers and striking “cantaloupe terrain,” patterned with mounds and pits. Scientists think overturning ice in the crust may have produced the terrain, but its precise origin remains uncertain.

key_facts.text: William Lassell discovered Triton on October 10, 1846, just 17 days after Neptune was discovered.
Triton has a retrograde orbit, moving around Neptune opposite the direction of the planet’s rotation.
Its unusual orbit supports the hypothesis that Triton was captured by Neptune from the Kuiper Belt; the exact origin scenario remains an inference.
Voyager 2 found active geysers on Triton during its 1989 flyby; its thin atmosphere is mostly nitrogen.
The unique cantaloupe terrain has irregular mounds; crustal overturn and rising blobs of ice are a proposed explanation for its formation.

overview.text: Red blood cells are specialized cells in the blood whose main job is to deliver oxygen from the lungs to tissues throughout the body. They also help carry carbon dioxide back to the lungs to be breathed out. Inside each cell, hemoglobin binds oxygen; its iron-containing heme helps give blood its red color. Red blood cells have a distinctive disk shape with a shallow indentation in the center. Bone marrow makes new blood cells to replace old ones, and a red blood cell typically lives for about 120 days before the spleen removes it. Their oxygen-delivery role makes them essential to the body’s tissues.

Hemoglobin inside red blood cells binds oxygen; its heme contains iron.

overview.text: Ammonia (NH₃) is a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, normally a colorless gas with a sharp, pungent odor. In water it acts as a weak base, accepting a hydrogen ion from water to form ammonium and hydroxide ions. This behavior helps make aqueous ammonia useful in cleaning products. Its largest industrial role is supplying nitrogen for fertilizers, supporting plant growth. Manufacturers synthesize it by reacting nitrogen and hydrogen at elevated temperature and pressure with an iron catalyst in the Haber–Bosch process. Ammonia is also used to make nitric acid, refrigerants, and other chemicals; if released or mismanaged, it can harm aquatic ecosystems.

In water, ammonia is a weak base: only some molecules react to form ammonium and hydroxide ions.

Ammonia is used in fertilizers and in making products including nitric acid, household cleaners, and refrigerants.
Ammonia entering surface waters can act as a nutrient, but high concentrations can harm aquatic life.

overview.text: Ludwig Boltzmann (1844–1906) was an Austrian physicist and a pioneer of atomic theory and statistical mechanics. He helped explain thermodynamic behavior by applying probability to the motions and possible arrangements of molecules. In his 1877 work, he connected the likelihood of a system’s overall state with how many microscopic arrangements could produce it; equilibrium corresponds to a highly probable state. The formula S = k log W is engraved on his tombstone, but Boltzmann did not write that exact formula himself. His work on gases, entropy, and irreversibility helped shape the statistical understanding of physical systems.

key_facts.text: Boltzmann was born in Vienna and lived from 1844 to 1906.
The University of Graz describes his work there as important to statistical heat theory and the interpretation of entropy and irreversibility, including the H-theorem.
In his 1877 combinatorial argument, Boltzmann treated equilibrium as the most probable overall state, related to the number of microscopic arrangements that can produce it.
The formula S = k log W is engraved on Boltzmann’s tombstone, but the Stanford Encyclopedia notes that he never wrote that exact formula down.
Boltzmann held professorships at the University of Graz twice, from 1869–1873 and 1876–1890.

overview.text: Boeing (The Boeing Company) is a U.S. aerospace company whose roots trace to William Boeing’s Seattle airplane business, incorporated as Pacific Aero Products in 1916. Today, it works across commercial aviation, defense, space systems, and support services, so its work ranges from passenger jets and freighters to military platforms and space technology. Familiar commercial aircraft include the 737, 777, and 787. Boeing also developed the CST-100 Starliner, a crew spacecraft for NASA’s Commercial Crew Program, designed to transport people and cargo to low Earth orbit and the International Space Station. This combination of airline-scale aircraft, defense systems, and spacecraft distinguishes Boeing from a company focused only on passenger planes.

overview.text: Cherenkov radiation is electromagnetic light produced when a charged particle moves through a transparent material faster than light’s phase speed in that material—not faster than light in a vacuum. The particle disturbs the material, and the resulting light waves form a forward-facing cone, somewhat like a sonic boom’s shock front. In water around a reactor, this can appear as a blue or violet glow. Because the cone’s angle depends on the particle’s speed, detectors can use the light to help measure speed and identify particles. Pavel Cherenkov observed the effect in 1934; Ilya Frank and Igor Tamm later explained it theoretically, and all three shared the 1958 Nobel Prize in Physics.

key_facts.text: The effect occurs when a charged particle travels faster than light does in a particular transparent material; it does not mean the particle exceeds light’s speed in a vacuum.
The emitted radiation forms a cone, and its angle depends on the particle’s speed.
The glow around a reactor can look blue or violet; the exact visible appearance is not the definition of the effect.
Cherenkov detectors use the emitted light to help measure particle speed and identify particles.

overview.text: Down syndrome (also called trisomy 21) is a genetic condition associated with extra genetic material from chromosome 21, one of the chromosomes that carries genes in the body’s cells. That extra material affects brain and body development, so people may have differences in learning and development and a higher chance of some health conditions; the effects vary from person to person, and many live healthy lives with supportive care. Most often, all cells have three separate copies of chromosome 21. Less commonly, the extra material is attached to another chromosome (translocation), or only some cells have it (mosaic trisomy 21). Most cases begin as a random cell-division event, not an action or fault of parents.

key_facts.text: Trisomy 21 is the pattern in which each cell has three separate copies of chromosome 21; it is the most common form of Down syndrome.
In mosaic Down syndrome, some cells have three copies of chromosome 21 while others have the usual two.
In translocation Down syndrome, extra chromosome 21 material is attached to another chromosome; in some cases, a parent without Down syndrome can carry a chromosome rearrangement that is passed on.
Most cases result from a random cell-division error called nondisjunction. NICHD says no parental behavior or environmental factor is known to cause Down syndrome.
Possible associated health conditions include congenital heart defects, hearing loss, and obstructive sleep apnea, but individuals’ traits and health needs vary.

overview.text: Inertial confinement fusion (ICF) is a method of initiating fusion by rapidly compressing and heating a tiny fuel target. Instead of using magnetic fields to hold plasma, it relies on the imploding fuel’s inertia to keep particles close enough for reactions before the fuel flies apart. In common laser-driven indirect-drive experiments, lasers heat a surrounding hollow metal cylinder, generating X-rays that strip material from the capsule’s surface and drive it inward; direct-drive designs illuminate the capsule directly. ICF matters for studying matter under extreme conditions and nuclear processes, and is investigated as a possible energy source. But producing fusion in experiments is not yet equivalent to a practical power plant.

key_facts.text: A common fuel is deuterium and tritium, two hydrogen isotopes; their fusion produces a helium nucleus and a neutron.
In indirect drive, a hohlraum converts laser energy into X-rays that compress the fuel capsule; direct drive focuses laser light on the capsule itself.
Inertial confinement works on an extremely brief timescale: DOE describes fuel compression to high densities for billionths of a second.
Fusion ignition in a laboratory is distinct from commercial power generation; developing a practical fusion energy system still involves scientific and technological challenges.
ICF research serves nuclear-stockpile stewardship as well as research into fusion’s potential role in energy production.

overview.text: Apoptosis (uh-POP-toh-sis) is a regulated form of cell death—often called programmed cell death—that helps a multicellular organism remove unneeded, damaged, or abnormal cells. It is important in development and tissue maintenance: for example, it helps remove tissue between developing digits. Caspases, enzymes activated in a controlled chain reaction, carry out much of the cell’s dismantling. Signals can start the process through cell-surface receptors or from within the cell; one internal pathway involves mitochondria releasing cytochrome c. As apoptosis proceeds, the cell shrinks, its DNA and nucleus fragment, and its membrane forms blebs and sealed pieces called apoptotic bodies. Nearby cells or macrophages engulf these fragments. Unlike cells that swell and burst after acute injury, apoptotic cells are dismantled in an orderly way.

key_facts.text: Apoptosis helps balance cell production and removal, maintaining adult tissues.
Caspases activate one another in a cascade and cleave proteins involved in cell breakdown.
In one internal pathway, mitochondrial cytochrome c helps activate caspase-9 with Apaf-1.
In *C. elegans*, 131 of 1,090 somatic cells are eliminated through programmed cell death during development.
Apoptosis may be blocked in cancer cells, allowing abnormal cells to persist.

overview.text: Fluorine is a chemical element with symbol F and atomic number 9. On the Pauling scale, it has the highest electronegativity value, meaning its atoms strongly attract shared electrons in chemical bonds. At room temperature, pure fluorine is a very pale yellow-green, highly reactive gas. This hazardous elemental form is different from fluoride, the negatively charged ion found in many compounds. Fluoride compounds are used in toothpaste and some drinking water to help prevent tooth decay. In the mouth, fluoride helps replace minerals lost when acids attack teeth and makes enamel harder to dissolve, showing how fluorine-containing compounds can have useful roles even though elemental fluorine is dangerous.

overview.text: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was a German philosopher, mathematician, and polymath whose work ranged across metaphysics, logic, and mathematics. A leading rationalist, he argued that reality is grounded in simple, immaterial substances called monads. Though they do not directly affect one another, God’s “pre-established harmony” makes their independent activity appear coordinated. In his 1710 Theodicy, Leibniz defended the religious-philosophical claim that God chose the best among possible worlds, addressing how evil could exist in such a world. He also developed calculus independently of Isaac Newton; Leibniz’s differential and integral notation helped shape the symbols still used in mathematics.

key_facts.text: He was born in Leipzig on 1 July 1646 and died in Hannover on 14 November 1716.
Leibniz’s monads were simple, immaterial substances that, in his theory, did not directly interact; their coordination was explained by pre-established harmony.

overview.text: The Arthaśāstra (also written Arthashastra) is a Sanskrit work on statecraft: how rulers organize and sustain a kingdom. Tradition associates it with Kautilya, also known as Chanakya, but scholars question who composed the surviving text and when. Its fifteen books range across royal administration, law, taxation and economic activity, diplomacy, espionage, and war. Rather than simply describing how a kingdom operated, the work offers practical guidance for governing, building resources, and dealing with rivals. Its wide-ranging treatment of political and economic questions makes it an important text for studying ancient South Asian political thought.

key_facts.text: The title is associated with material gain or the science of polity; the work focuses on governing a state, not just personal wealth.
Kautilya is the traditional author; the surviving text’s authorship and development remain debated.
The work is a guide to statecraft, not a direct historical account of Mauryan administration.
Its topics include organizing government, raising revenue, maintaining law and order, and settling disputes.

overview.text: The Federal Reserve System, usually called the Federal Reserve or “the Fed,” is the central bank of the United States. Congress created it in 1913 to help provide a safer, more flexible, and more stable monetary and financial system. Its distinctive hybrid structure combines a Board of Governors in Washington, 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks, and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). The FOMC sets monetary policy, while the broader system also supervises banks, monitors financial-system risks, and supports payment services. The regional network gives the Fed a decentralized operating structure, while the Board provides oversight and the System remains accountable to Congress.

key_facts.text: President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act into law on December 23, 1913, creating the Federal Reserve System.
The System’s three key entities are the Board of Governors, 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks, and the FOMC.
The FOMC is the monetary-policy decision-making body; Congress has directed the Fed to pursue maximum employment and stable prices.
The Fed also supervises and regulates certain financial institutions, monitors financial stability, and helps operate payment systems.

overview.text: Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) was an American philosopher, logician, and working scientist whose career joined abstract reasoning with hands-on measurement: for 32 years he worked for the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey. He is recognized as the principal originator of pragmatism, a philosophical method he first developed in publications of the 1870s; William James later helped popularize the movement. Peirce’s distinctive pragmatic maxim asks us to clarify an idea by considering the practical, observable consequences we would expect if it were true—not simply by repeating a definition. He applied this approach to scientific inquiry, and also developed influential work on logic and the theory of signs; later, he called his view “pragmaticism.”

key_facts.text: Peirce was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1839 and died in 1914.
His 1878 essay “How to Make Our Ideas Clear” gives a canonical statement of the pragmatic maxim.
Peirce worked for the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey for 32 years, conducting geodetic investigations and scientific measurements.
His work ranged beyond pragmatism and logic to a general theory of signs, often called “semeiotic.”

overview.text: Philip Zimbardo’s 2007 nonfiction book *The Lucifer Effect: Understanding How Good People Turn Evil* asks how ordinary people can take part in cruelty. It argues that situations, group dynamics, and larger systems—not only individual character—can influence harmful behavior. The book’s central case is Zimbardo’s account of the 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment, which he connects to prisoner abuse at Abu Ghraib, Iraq; it also considers ways people can resist harmful pressures and act heroically. A distinctive feature is this pairing of a prison simulation with a real-world abuse case. Readers should treat the book’s interpretation of the Stanford study as debated: later archival scholarship questioned its scientific validity and described concerns about how it was conducted.
